Replace.Text: The kurofune – the “black ships” of European and American powers – came as shocks to Edo Japan. While Edo was a stable, prosperous place, it lagged behind in industrial advancements, and Japanese leaders realized that they needed to modernize if they were to remain independent – an impulse that would eventually give rise to the Meiji Restoration. Nirayama Reverberatory Furnace was one place where this industrialization was enacted.

Built off of Dutch models, the furnace was completed in 1855-1857 CE. Its design involves keeping the furnace – beneath the two iconic smokestacks – separate from the iron, allowing the metal to melt without the introduction of by-products from the forge. Molten metal would then pour into molds in a central pit – molds, especially, of cannons. A Japan that was to defend against the kurofune would need its naval armaments.

Ancient Korea was divided into three kingdoms: northern Goguryeo, southern Silla, and western Baekje (near present-day Seoul). Though Silla, the smallest of these, was to dominate the peninsula in later years, Baekje made aggressive advances in military conquest, in diplomacy (opening ties with China and Japan), and in establishing a cultural footprint. And here is where Mireuksa enters the story.

Buddhism came to Baekje in 385 CE and, like elsewhere in the region, became closely associated with the power of the monarchy. Visiting a lake in the southern part of Baekje, King Mu received a vision of the Maitreya Buddha (the Buddha who is to come). Mu had the water drained and constructed on the site a temple complex including two stone pagodas and a massive wooden building linked by a covered hall. Gold plaques professing the monarchs’ devotion to Buddhism were installed at the site, though the original woodworking has long since disappeared.

One of Japan’s tallest waterfalls, Nachi Falls is both a place of natural beauty and religious pilgrimage. Water drops uninterrupted over 430 feet, providing a backdrop for both a Shinto shrine and Buddhist temple. Within the context of Japanese religion, this is unsurprising – places of natural beauty and wonder are the homes of the kami, the Shinto gods, as beauty in the seen world reflects beauty in the unseen world. The falls are in Japan’s south, in Kii province.

If Jeju Island is the pinnacle of Korea’s natural beauty, the volcanic crater of Seongsan Ilchubong has a good deal to do with it. The rounded cup rising 300 feet above the sea resembles, to Korean observers, a fortress – and, in fact, during the Japanese occupation of Korea the mountain was the site of defensive fortifications remaining today. Seongsan Ilchubong remains a popular site to view the sunrise on the island, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Mireuksa
